executiveSummary: Chapter 17 covers the classification, measurement, and reporting of debt and equity investments under IFRS 9, using a mixed-attribute model that values some instruments at amortized cost and others at fair value. The chapter concludes that while fair value provides the most relevant information for financial statement users, a business-model-based approach determines which measurement applies, with unrealized gains and losses routed either through net income or other comprehensive income depending on investment type and intent. Appendices extend the discussion to derivative financial instruments and the three-level fair value disclosure hierarchy.
keyTopics: Classification and measurement of debt investments: IFRS 9 requires companies to evaluate two criteria—the business model for managing the investment and whether contractual cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest—to determine if a debt investment is carried at amortized cost (held-for-collection) or fair value (held-for-collection and selling, or trading).

Held-for-collection (HFC) debt investments: These are measured at amortized cost using the effective-interest method to amortize any premium or discount; interest revenue is recognised each period, and gains/losses on early sale are reported in income.

Held-for-collection and selling (HFCS) debt investments: Reported at fair value on the statement of financial position, with unrealized holding gains and losses recorded in other comprehensive income (OCI) and accumulated in equity; realised gains/losses are recycled to the income statement upon sale.

Trading debt investments: Reported at fair value with all unrealized holding gains and losses recognised directly in net income each period, reflecting the intent to profit from short-term price changes.

Equity investments and ownership thresholds: Holdings below 20% are generally accounted for at fair value (trading = unrealized gains/losses through income; non-trading election = unrealized gains/losses through OCI); holdings of 20–50% use the equity method; holdings above 50% require consolidated financial statements.

Equity method of accounting: The investor records the investment at cost and subsequently adjusts the carrying amount for its proportionate share of the investee's net income or loss; dividends received reduce the carrying amount rather than being recorded as revenue.

Impairment of investments: For HFC debt investments, the expected credit loss (ECL) model is used; the impairment loss is measured as the difference between the carrying amount and the present value of revised expected cash flows discounted at the historical effective-interest rate, with reversal permitted under IFRS if credit quality improves.

Derivative financial instruments and hedging (Appendix 17A): Derivatives are recognised at fair value on the statement of financial position; gains/losses on speculative derivatives go through income; fair value hedges record both the derivative and the hedged item at fair value in income; cash flow hedges record derivative gains/losses in OCI until the hedged transaction affects earnings.

importantDefinitions.Amortized cost: The initial recognition amount of a financial asset minus principal repayments, plus or minus cumulative amortization of any premium or discount, net of any allowance for impairment.
importantDefinitions.Fair value: The amount for which an asset could be exchanged between knowledgeable, willing parties in an arm's length transaction; under IFRS, equivalent to the price received to sell an asset in an orderly market transaction at the measurement date.
importantDefinitions.Held-for-collection (HFC): A debt investment category where the company's business model is to hold the asset to collect contractual cash flows (principal and interest) over the investment's life; measured at amortized cost.
importantDefinitions.Held-for-collection and selling (HFCS): A debt investment category where the objective is both to collect contractual cash flows and to sell the securities; measured at fair value with unrealized gains/losses in OCI.
importantDefinitions.Trading investments: Debt or equity investments bought and held primarily for sale in the near term to generate profits from short-term price differences; reported at fair value with unrealized gains/losses in net income.
importantDefinitions.Equity method: An accounting approach used when an investor has significant influence (generally 20–50% ownership) over an investee; the investment is initially recorded at cost and adjusted each period for the investor's share of the investee's net income or loss, with dividends reducing the carrying amount.
importantDefinitions.Significant influence: The power to participate in the financial and operating policy decisions of an investee without controlling those decisions; generally presumed when an investor holds 20% or more of the voting shares.
importantDefinitions.Unrealized holding gain or loss: The net change in fair value of a security from one period to the next, exclusive of dividend or interest revenue recognized; reported in net income (trading) or OCI (HFCS and non-trading equity), depending on classification.
importantDefinitions.Expected credit loss (ECL) model: An impairment model under IFRS 9 that requires recognition of credit losses based on probability-weighted expected cash shortfalls, using either 12-month expected losses (no significant credit deterioration) or lifetime expected losses (significant credit deterioration).
importantDefinitions.Recycling adjustment: A reclassification entry that transfers previously recognised unrealized gains or losses out of accumulated OCI into net income when a security classified as HFCS is sold, preventing double-counting of gains/losses in comprehensive income.
importantDefinitions.Derivative financial instrument: A financial contract whose value is derived from an underlying variable (share price, interest rate, commodity price, etc.); characterised by an underlying, little or no initial investment, and future settlement.
importantDefinitions.Fair value option: An irrevocable election available at initial recognition to measure most financial instruments at fair value, with all subsequent gains and losses reported in net income, typically used to eliminate an accounting mismatch between an asset and a related liability.

accountingTreatments: Debt investment—HFC (amortized cost): Debit Debt Investments at purchase price; each period debit Cash and credit Interest Revenue for cash received, and adjust the carrying amount for discount/premium amortization using the effective-interest method (e.g., Robinson SA: debit Debt Investments €92,278, credit Cash €92,278 at purchase; debit Cash €4,000 and Debt Investments €614, credit Interest Revenue €4,614 on July 1, 2022).

Debt investment—HFCS (fair value through OCI): Record at purchase price; amortize discount or premium each period; at reporting date, adjust to fair value via a Fair Value Adjustment valuation account and record the unrealized gain or loss in Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss—Equity (e.g., Graff plc: Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss—Equity 1,732 / Fair Value Adjustment 1,732 at December 31, 2022). On sale, recognise the realised gain/loss in income and make a recycling adjustment to eliminate the prior OCI balance.

Debt investment—Trading (fair value through income): At each reporting date, adjust the portfolio to fair value via the Fair Value Adjustment account with the offset to Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss—Income, which flows through net income (e.g., Western Publishing: Fair Value Adjustment 3,750 / Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss—Income 3,750).

Equity investment—Trading (<20%, fair value through income): Record at cost (broker commissions expensed); recognise dividends as revenue when declared; at period-end adjust to fair value, debiting or crediting Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss—Income (e.g., Republic SA: Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss—Income 35,550 / Fair Value Adjustment 35,550 for net unrealized loss).

Equity investment—Non-trading option (fair value through OCI): Same as trading but unrealized gains/losses are recorded in Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss—Equity (OCI); upon sale, the carrying amount equals fair value so no separate gain/loss is recognised in income, and the accumulated OCI balance may be transferred to retained earnings (not recycled to income).

Equity method (20–50% ownership): Record investment at cost; each period debit Equity Investments and credit Investment Income for the investor's share of investee net income (e.g., Maxi: Investment Income = 20% × Mini's net income); dividends received debit Cash and credit Equity Investments; if losses exceed the carrying amount, stop recognising further losses unless the investor has committed to providing further support.
criticalFormulas: Effective-Interest Revenue on Debt Investment: Interest Revenue = Beginning Carrying Amount × Effective (Yield) Rate × Time Fraction. Variables: Beginning Carrying Amount = amortized cost at start of period; Effective Rate = yield rate at acquisition; Time Fraction = portion of year. Example: Robinson SA, July 1, 2022 — Interest Revenue = €92,278 × 10% × 6/12 = €4,614.

Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss (Portfolio Adjustment): Fair Value Adjustment (Debit or Credit) = [Aggregate Fair Value of Portfolio] − [Aggregate Amortized Cost of Portfolio] − [Existing Fair Value Adjustment Balance]. Example: Webb AG 2022 HFCS portfolio: aggregate unrealized loss = −€9,537; prior balance = 0; entry = Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss—Equity 9,537 / Fair Value Adjustment 9,537.

Gain or Loss on Sale of Debt Investment: Gain (Loss) = Selling Price (net of accrued interest) − Book Value (amortized cost) at date of sale. Example: Robinson SA sells Evermaster bonds Nov. 1, 2024: Selling price = €99,750; Book value ≈ €98,675 (after amortization to Nov. 1); Gain ≈ €1,075.

Impairment Loss on HFC Debt Investment: Loss = Carrying Amount − Present Value of Revised Expected Cash Flows (discounted at historical effective-interest rate). Example: Mayhew Ltd.: Carrying amount = ¥200,000; PV of revised cash flows = ¥187,320 (¥136,602 principal + ¥50,718 interest annuity); Impairment Loss = ¥200,000 − ¥187,320 = ¥12,680.

Equity Method Income Recognition: Investment Income = Investor's Ownership % × Investee's Net Income (or Net Loss). Example: Maxi Company (20% of Mini): Mini reports €100,000 net income; Maxi records Investment Income = 20% × €100,000 = €20,000; debit Equity Investments €20,000, credit Investment Income €20,000.
illustrativeExample: Robinson SA purchases €100,000, 8% bonds of Evermaster AG on January 1, 2022, for €92,278 (discount; yield 10%); classified as held-for-collection. Step 1 — Purchase: Debt Investments 92,278 / Cash 92,278. Step 2 — July 1, 2022 interest receipt: Cash 4,000 / Debt Investments 614 / Interest Revenue 4,614 (carrying amount rises to €92,892). Step 3 — December 31, 2022 accrual: Interest Receivable 4,000 / Debt Investments 645 / Interest Revenue 4,645. Step 4 — Income statement 2022: Interest Revenue = €4,614 + €4,645 = €9,259. Step 5 — Early sale (Nov. 1, 2024) at 99¾ plus accrued interest: Cash (€99,750 + €2,667) / Interest Revenue 2,667 / Debt Investments [book value] / Gain on Sale of Investments [difference]; gain reflects excess of selling price over amortized book value.
disclosurePresentationNotes: Statement of financial position classification: Debt investments at amortized cost (HFC) and at fair value (HFCS, trading) are presented as long-term investments; related interest receivable appears as a current asset; the Fair Value Adjustment valuation account adjusts the carrying amount to fair value for HFCS and trading portfolios.

OCI and equity presentation: Unrealized holding gains and losses on HFCS debt investments and non-trading equity investments are reported as a separate component of other comprehensive income and accumulated in equity as Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI); the components must be disclosed, including any recycling (reclassification) adjustments.

Fair value hierarchy disclosures (Appendix 17B): Companies must disclose fair values and the corresponding hierarchy level—Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (observable inputs for similar instruments), and Level 3 (unobservable/internal inputs); for Level 3 instruments, a roll-forward reconciliation of beginning to ending balances and a description of valuation techniques and significant unobservable inputs are required.

Impairment disclosures: Companies must disclose the methodology used to identify and measure impairments, including use of the ECL model; for HFCS investments, the portion of a fair value decline attributable to credit risk (reported in income) must be separated from fair value changes due to market interest rate movements (reported in OCI).
potentialPitfalls: Confusing the routing of unrealized gains and losses: Trading debt/equity investments route unrealized gains and losses through net income, while HFCS debt investments and non-trading equity investments route them through OCI. A common error is applying income treatment to HFCS securities or failing to use the separate Fair Value Adjustment account (instead directly crediting the investment account), which destroys the amortized cost record needed for effective-interest calculations.

Forgetting the recycling adjustment for HFCS securities upon sale: When an HFCS bond is sold, the realised gain/loss enters net income, but the same amount was previously recognised in OCI. Without a reclassification (recycling) entry or note disclosure, the gain/loss is double-counted in comprehensive income across periods. Non-trading equity investments are explicitly not recycled under IFRS—this asymmetry with HFCS debt is another source of confusion.

Misapplying the equity method versus fair value when ownership is near 20%: The 20% threshold is a rebuttable presumption, not a hard rule; evidence of significant influence (board representation, policy participation, material intercompany transactions) can require equity method accounting even below 20%, while lack of influence can preclude it above 20%. Additionally, equity method investors must stop recognising further losses once the carrying amount reaches zero (unless they have guaranteed the investee's obligations), a step frequently overlooked.
